narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 74.7% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction as a key factor, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three aspects of your academic record. Your class rank at the end of your third year was the strongest factor pushing the model toward predicting failure. Standing in only the second decile, noticeably below the average of accepted students (around the sixth decile), signaled to the model that your performance placed you at higher risk of struggling with the bar. Your first-year class rank was the third most important factor and also pulled the prediction toward failure; at the third decile, it was well below the sixth-decile average of accepted applicants.

Your LSAT score was the second most influential piece of information, but it worked in the opposite direction. At 38, you scored slightly above the average of accepted students (37.18), which gave the model some confidence that you could succeed. Unfortunately, this positive signal was not strong enough to outweigh the two weaker academic rankings.

Given these results, you should focus on strengthening your academic trajectory and bar-exam readiness. Consider retaking key courses to improve your class standing, investing additional time in structured bar-prep programs, or gaining practical legal experience that demonstrates your ability to handle rigorous material. With targeted improvement, your profile could look much stronger for future applications. (248 words)
